claim: Malaria is transmitted when an infected Anopheles mosquito deposits Plasmodium sporozoites in the skin during a bite.
source: Malaria is transmitted when an infected Anopheles mosquito deposits Plasmodium sporozoites in the skin during a bite.
evidence: This is established knowledge about malaria transmission.

claim: Sporozoites are formed within oocysts at the mosquito midgut wall.
source: Sporozoites are formed within oocysts at the mosquito midgut wall and are released into the hemolymph, from where they invade the salivary glands and are subsequently transmitted to the vertebrate host.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Plasmodium life cycle.

claim: Sporozoites are released from oocysts into the hemolymph.
source: Sporozoites are formed within oocysts at the mosquito midgut wall and are released into the hemolymph, from where they invade the salivary glands and are subsequently transmitted to the vertebrate host.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Plasmodium life cycle.

claim: Sporozoites invade the salivary glands from the hemolymph.
source: Sporozoites are formed within oocysts at the mosquito midgut wall and are released into the hemolymph, from where they invade the salivary glands and are subsequently transmitted to the vertebrate host.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Plasmodium life cycle.

claim: TRP1 is important for oocyst egress.
source: We found that a thrombospondin-repeat containing sporozoite-specific protein named thrombospondin-releated protein 1 (TRP1) is important for oocyst egress and salivary gland invasion, and hence for the transmission of malaria.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data showing trp1(-) parasites fail to egress from oocysts.

claim: TRP1 is important for salivary gland invasion.
source: We found that a thrombospondin-repeat containing sporozoite-specific protein named thrombospondin-releated protein 1 (TRP1) is important for oocyst egress and salivary gland invasion, and hence for the transmission of malaria.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data showing no salivary gland sporozoites in trp1(-) parasites.

claim: TRP1 is important for the transmission of malaria.
source: We found that a thrombospondin-repeat containing sporozoite-specific protein named thrombospondin-releated protein 1 (TRP1) is important for oocyst egress and salivary gland invasion, and hence for the transmission of malaria.
evidence: This is inferred from the finding that TRP1 is required for oocyst egress and salivary gland invasion, which are necessary for transmission.

claim: The release of sporozoites from oocysts was imaged in situ.
source: We imaged the release of sporozoites from oocysts in situ, which was preceded by active motility.
evidence: This is a methodological achievement described in the manuscript with supporting video data.

claim: Active motility precedes sporozoite release from oocysts.
source: We imaged the release of sporozoites from oocysts in situ, which was preceded by active motility.
evidence: This is a primary observation from the imaging experiments.

claim: Parasites lacking TRP1 failed to migrate within oocysts.
source: Parasites lacking TRP1 failed to migrate within oocysts and did not egress, suggesting that TRP1 is a vital component of the events that precede intra-oocyst motility and subsequently sporozoite egress and salivary gland invasion.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the motility assays and imaging experiments.

claim: Parasites lacking TRP1 did not egress from oocysts.
source: Parasites lacking TRP1 failed to migrate within oocysts and did not egress, suggesting that TRP1 is a vital component of the events that precede intra-oocyst motility and subsequently sporozoite egress and salivary gland invasion.
evidence: This is a primary finding from sporozoite counting experiments.

claim: TRP1 is a vital component of the events that precede intra-oocyst motility.
source: Parasites lacking TRP1 failed to migrate within oocysts and did not egress, suggesting that TRP1 is a vital component of the events that precede intra-oocyst motility and subsequently sporozoite egress and salivary gland invasion.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: A single Plasmodium parasite that establishes itself in the mosquito gut is enough to form an extracellular oocyst.
source: A single Plasmodium parasite that establishes itself in the mosquito gut is enough to form an extracellular oocyst, in which hundreds of sporozoites can develop to colonize the salivary gland and be injected back into the vertebrate host.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Plasmodium biology.

claim: Hundreds of sporozoites can develop within an oocyst.
source: A single Plasmodium parasite that establishes itself in the mosquito gut is enough to form an extracellular oocyst, in which hundreds of sporozoites can develop to colonize the salivary gland and be injected back into the vertebrate host.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Plasmodium biology.

claim: A single sporozoite that successfully enters a hepatocyte is enough to produce thousands of progeny red-blood-cell-invading merozoites.
source: In Plasmodium species that infect mammals, a single sporozoite that successfully enters a hepatocyte is enough to produce thousands of progeny red-blood-cell-invading merozoites that then cause a full infection.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Plasmodium liver stage development.

claim: The release of parasites is dependent on a common set of specific proteins encoded by the parasite, including different proteases especially of the SERA family.
source: There is evidence from all three stages to show that the release of parasites is dependent on a common set of specific proteins encoded by the parasite, including different proteases especially of the SERA family (Arisue et al., 2007; Roiko and Carruthers, 2009) but also other factors with no or unknown enzymatic activity (Roiko and Carruthers, 2009; Wirth and Pradel, 2012; Talman et al., 2011; Ponzi et al., 2009; de Koning-Ward et al., 2008; Ishino et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Egress from blood cells and hepatocytes has been filmed in spectacular detail.
source: Egress from blood cells and hepatocytes has been filmed in spectacular detail (Abkarian et al., 2011; Sturm et al., 2006), and exflagellation of microgametes has been studied extensively by light and electron microscopy (Sinden et al., 1976; Deligianni et al., 2013; Wirth et al., 2014; Wilson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Exflagellation of microgametes has been studied extensively by light and electron microscopy.
source: Egress from blood cells and hepatocytes has been filmed in spectacular detail (Abkarian et al., 2011; Sturm et al., 2006), and exflagellation of microgametes has been studied extensively by light and electron microscopy (Sinden et al., 1976; Deligianni et al., 2013; Wirth et al., 2014; Wilson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: There is no live visual information about sporozoite egress from oocysts prior to this study.
source: By contrast, we have no live visual information about sporozoite egress from oocysts.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Electron microscopy images show that sporozoites can appear in holes within the oocyst wall and the basal lamina that surrounds the oocysts.
source: Indeed, despite the adaptation of new dynamic imaging approaches in parasite biology (Frischknecht, 2010; De Niz et al., 2017; Amino and Suzuki, 2014), the only evidence to show how sporozoites egress from oocysts are images from electron microscopy. These show that sporozoites can appear in holes within the oocyst wall and the basal lamina that surrounds the oocysts (Strome and Beaudoin, 1974; Meis et al., 1992; Sinden and Strong, 1978), but also suggest that oocysts could rupture to release many parasites simultaneoulsly (Meis et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous electron microscopy studies.

claim: Electron microscopy images suggest that oocysts could rupture to release many parasites simultaneously.
source: Indeed, despite the adaptation of new dynamic imaging approaches in parasite biology (Frischknecht, 2010; De Niz et al., 2017; Amino and Suzuki, 2014), the only evidence to show how sporozoites egress from oocysts are images from electron microscopy. These show that sporozoites can appear in holes within the oocyst wall and the basal lamina that surrounds the oocysts (Strome and Beaudoin, 1974; Meis et al., 1992; Sinden and Strong, 1978), but also suggest that oocysts could rupture to release many parasites simultaneoulsly (Meis et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous electron microscopy studies.

claim: Different Plasmodium species might use or prefer different ways to egress from oocysts.
source: Different species might use or prefer different ways to egress (Orfano et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Sporozoites lacking TRAP fail to undergo productive motility and salivary gland invasion.
source: Curiously, parasites lacking the thrombospondin-related anonymous protein (TRAP) also fail to undergo productive motility and salivary gland invasion, yet they have no defect in egress from oocysts (Sultan et al., 1997; Münter et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Sporozoites lacking TRAP have no defect in egress from oocysts.
source: Curiously, parasites lacking the thrombospondin-related anonymous protein (TRAP) also fail to undergo productive motility and salivary gland invasion, yet they have no defect in egress from oocysts (Sultan et al., 1997; Münter et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Sporozoites that lack TRAP are still able to perform forms of unproductive movement, during which the parasite is attached at one focal spot to the substrate.
source: Nevertheless, sporozoites that lack TRAP are still able to perform forms of unproductive movement, during which the parasite is attached at one focal spot to the substrate (Münter et al., 2009), which might be sufficient to force egress from oocysts.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: MTRAP is crucial for the egress of gametocytes from host cells.
source: It was recently shown that the TRAP-family member MTRAP, previously thought to be important for red blood cell invasion by merozoites, is crucial for the egress of gametocytes from host cells (Kehrer et al., 2016a; Bargieri et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: TRP1 carries a single thrombospondin repeat.
source: This revealed an as yet uncharacterized protein that carries a single thrombospondin repeat, one of the two adhesive domains found in TRAP-family members.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis of the protein sequence.

claim: TRP1 shares a transmembrane domain with TRAP-family proteins.
source: This thrombospondin-related protein 1, TRP1, also shared a transmembrane domain and a similar cytoplasmic tail with TRAP-family proteins (Figure 1).
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis and shown in Figure 1.

claim: TRP1 shares a similar cytoplasmic tail with TRAP-family proteins.
source: This thrombospondin-related protein 1, TRP1, also shared a transmembrane domain and a similar cytoplasmic tail with TRAP-family proteins (Figure 1).
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis and shown in Figure 1.

claim: Isolated trp1(-) sporozoites can undergo motility.
source: Intriguingly, isolated trp1(-) sporozoites can undergo motility, suggesting that TRP1 might play a role in activating sporozoite motility in vivo prior to egress from oocysts.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the motility assays.

claim: TRP1 might play a role in activating sporozoite motility in vivo prior to egress from oocysts.
source: Intriguingly, isolated trp1(-) sporozoites can undergo motility, suggesting that TRP1 might play a role in activating sporozoite motility in vivo prior to egress from oocysts.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: TRP1 contains a signal peptide.
source: Both TRP1 and TRAP contain a signal peptide (SP), a TSR, a transmembrane domain (TMD) and a cytoplasmic tail domain (CTD) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: TRP1 lacks the penultimate tryptophan that has been shown to be important for TRAP function.
source: However, TRP1 lacks the penultimate tryptophan (W) that has been shown to be important for TRAP function (Kappe et al., 1999) as well as the von Willebrandt factor like A-domain that is present at the N-terminus of TRAP and important for invasion (Matuschewski et al., 2002).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and comparison with TRAP, with citations to previous studies on TRAP function.

claim: TRP1 lacks the von Willebrandt factor like A-domain that is present at the N-terminus of TRAP and important for invasion.
source: However, TRP1 lacks the penultimate tryptophan (W) that has been shown to be important for TRAP function (Kappe et al., 1999) as well as the von Willebrandt factor like A-domain that is present at the N-terminus of TRAP and important for invasion (Matuschewski et al., 2002).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and comparison with TRAP, with citations to previous studies on TRAP function.

claim: The N-terminal domain of TRP1 is less conserved and varies widely in length between different Plasmodium species.
source: In comparison to that of TRAP, the N-terminal domain of TRP1 is less conserved and varies widely in length between different Plasmodium species (332 aa in P. vivax; 651 aa in P. falciparum) (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis across Plasmodium species.

claim: The TSR of TRP1 is well conserved.
source: By contrast, the TSR of TRP1 is well conserved but has an unusual long insertion of 10 amino acids when compared to TSRs from other apicomplexan proteins (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The TSR of TRP1 has an unusual long insertion of 10 amino acids when compared to TSRs from other apicomplexan proteins.
source: By contrast, the TSR of TRP1 is well conserved but has an unusual long insertion of 10 amino acids when compared to TSRs from other apicomplexan proteins (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The calculated isoelectric point (pI) of the CTD of TRP1 varied widely between homologues from different Plasmodium species.
source: However, the calculated isoelectric point (pI) of the CTD of TRP1 varied widely between homologues from different Plasmodium species and indicated no enrichment for acidic amino acids (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is based on computational analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The CTD of TRP1 shows no enrichment for acidic amino acids.
source: However, the calculated isoelectric point (pI) of the CTD of TRP1 varied widely between homologues from different Plasmodium species and indicated no enrichment for acidic amino acids (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is based on computational analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Homologues of TRP1 can be found in all Plasmodium species.
source: Homologues of TRP1 can be found in all Plasmodium species, but we could not identify homologues in other apicomplexans.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic searches across species.

claim: Homologues of TRP1 could not be identified in other apicomplexans.
source: Homologues of TRP1 can be found in all Plasmodium species, but we could not identify homologues in other apicomplexans.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic searches across species.

claim: Expression of mCherry in trp1(-)mCh parasites was only observed in budding and completely sporulated oocysts up to hemolymph sporozoites.
source: Expression of mCherry in trp1(-)mCh parasites was only observed in budding and completely sporulated oocysts up to hemolymph sporozoites (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a primary observation from fluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Oocyst numbers for the control decreased between day 12 and day 22.
source: Oocyst numbers for the control decreased between day 12 and day 22, whereas the number of oocysts in infected trp1(-)mCh mosquitoes remained stable.
evidence: This is a primary finding from oocyst counting experiments shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The number of oocysts in infected trp1(-)mCh mosquitoes remained stable between day 12 and day 22.
source: Oocyst numbers for the control decreased between day 12 and day 22, whereas the number of oocysts in infected trp1(-)mCh mosquitoes remained stable.
evidence: This is a primary finding from oocyst counting experiments shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Over 80% of the trp1(-)mCh oocysts were sporulated on day 22 compared with just 45% in the control line.
source: While there was only a slight difference in this ratio between control and knockout on day 12, over 80% of the trp1(-)mCh oocysts were sporulated on day 22 compared with just 45% in the control line.
evidence: This is a primary finding from oocyst imaging and classification shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Mosquitoes infected with both trp1(-) knockout lines could not transmit the parasites to mice.
source: These experiments showed that mosquitoes infected with both knockout lines could not transmit the parasites to mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding from transmission experiments shown in Table 3.

claim: There was no difference in prepatencies between wild-type and trp1(-) parasites if midgut sporozoites were injected intravenously.
source: However, we observed no difference in prepatencies between wild-type and trp1(-) parasites if midgut sporozoites were injected intravenously.
evidence: This is a primary finding from sporozoite injection experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Mosquitoes that are infected with trp1(-) or trp1(-)mCh consistently showed high numbers of midgut sporozoites until 22 days post infection.
source: By contrast, mosquitoes that are infected with trp1(-) or trp1(-)mCh consistently showed high numbers of midgut sporozoites until 22 days post infection, while we observed only few sporozoites in the hemolymph and none in salivary glands (Table 2, Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from sporozoite counting experiments shown in Table 2 and Figure 3A.

claim: Mosquitoes infected with trp1(-) or trp1(-)mCh showed only few sporozoites in the hemolymph.
source: By contrast, mosquitoes that are infected with trp1(-) or trp1(-)mCh consistently showed high numbers of midgut sporozoites until 22 days post infection, while we observed only few sporozoites in the hemolymph and none in salivary glands (Table 2, Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from sporozoite counting experiments shown in Table 2 and Figure 3A.

claim: Mosquitoes infected with trp1(-) or trp1(-)mCh showed no sporozoites in salivary glands.
source: By contrast, mosquitoes that are infected with trp1(-) or trp1(-)mCh consistently showed high numbers of midgut sporozoites until 22 days post infection, while we observed only few sporozoites in the hemolymph and none in salivary glands (Table 2, Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from sporozoite counting experiments shown in Table 2 and Figure 3A.

claim: Both wild-type and trp1(-) sporozoites derived from midguts were able to perform the typical circular gliding motility of sporozoites but at very low rates (ca. 0.5–1% of the population) on day 15.
source: Both wild-type and trp1(-) sporozoites derived from midguts were able to perform the typical circular gliding motility of sporozoites (Vanderberg, 1974) but at very low rates (ca. 0.5–1% of the population) on day 15 (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from motility assays shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The fraction of motile sporozoites increased in hemolymph sporozoites to 10–20% of the population.
source: This fraction increased in hemolymph sporozoites to 10–20% of the population, and again, no significant difference between trp1(-) and wild-type sporozoites was observed (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: This is a primary finding from motility assays shown in Figure 3E,F.

claim: No significant difference in motility between trp1(-) and wild-type hemolymph sporozoites was observed.
source: This fraction increased in hemolymph sporozoites to 10–20% of the population, and again, no significant difference between trp1(-) and wild-type sporozoites was observed (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: This is a primary finding from motility assays shown in Figure 3E,F.

claim: The fraction of motile midgut sporozoites increased in the trp1(-)mCh line over time and reached a level comparable to that of wild-type hemolymph sporozoites at day 22 post infection.
source: Interestingly the fraction of motile midgut sporozoites increased in the trp1(-)mCh line over time and reached a level comparable to that of wild-type hemolymph sporozoites at day 22 post infection (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: This is a primary finding from motility assays shown in Figure 3D,E.

claim: No difference in the percentage of moving midgut wild-type sporozoites was observed between day 15 and day 25.
source: By contrast, we observed no difference in the percentage of moving midgut wild-type sporozoites between day 15 and day 25 (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from motility assays shown in Figure 3D.

claim: gfp-trp1comp and gfp-trp1 parasites showed normal ratios of HLS to MGS as well as of SGS to MGS that were comparable to wt.
source: Both, gfp-trp1comp and gfp-trp1 parasites showed normal ratios of HLS to MGS as well as of SGS to MGS that were comparable to wt (Figure 4A,B, Table 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding from sporozoite counting experiments shown in Figure 4A,B and Table 2.

claim: gfp-trp1comp parasites showed fully restored capacity to egress and invade.
source: The observed sporozoites numbers in midgut, hemolymph and salivary glands between day 18 and day 22 in mosquitoes infected with gfp-trp1comp indicate the fully restored capacity to egress and invade (Figure 4C,D, Table 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding from sporozoite counting experiments shown in Figure 4C,D and Table 2.

claim: gfp-trp1∆N sporozoites are more capable of egressing from oocysts than gfp-trp1∆C sporozoites.
source: This suggests that gfp-trp1∆N sporozoites are more capable of egressing from oocysts than gfp-trp1∆C sporozoites.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the sporozoite counting data shown in Figure 4A and Table 2.

claim: The ratio of SGS to MGS was zero for both gfp-trp1∆C and gfp-trp1∆N.
source: By contrast, the ratio of SGS to MGS was zero for both gfp-trp1∆C and gfp-trp1∆N, indicating that the knockout phenotype is only partially restored in gfp-trp1∆N parasites.
evidence: This is a primary finding from sporozoite counting experiments shown in Figure 4B and Table 2.

claim: The knockout phenotype is only partially restored in gfp-trp1∆N parasites.
source: By contrast, the ratio of SGS to MGS was zero for both gfp-trp1∆C and gfp-trp1∆N, indicating that the knockout phenotype is only partially restored in gfp-trp1∆N parasites.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the sporozoite counting data shown in Figure 4B and Table 2.

claim: gfp-trp1comp and gfp-trp1 showed normal infectivity in mice.
source: While gfp-trp1comp and gfp-trp1 showed normal infectivity in mice, no infection could be observed for gfp-trp1∆N and gfp-trp1∆C.
evidence: This is a primary finding from transmission experiments shown in Table 3 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: No infection could be observed for gfp-trp1∆N and gfp-trp1∆C in transmission experiments.
source: While gfp-trp1comp and gfp-trp1 showed normal infectivity in mice, no infection could be observed for gfp-trp1∆N and gfp-trp1∆C.
evidence: This is a primary finding from transmission experiments shown in Table 3 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The N-terminus of TRP1 is important for oocyst egress.
source: These data suggest that the N-terminus of TRP1 is important for oocyst egress and that both the N- and the C-terminus are essential for salivary gland invasion.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the complementation experiments with truncated TRP1 mutants.

claim: Both the N- and the C-terminus of TRP1 are essential for salivary gland invasion.
source: These data suggest that the N-terminus of TRP1 is important for oocyst egress and that both the N- and the C-terminus are essential for salivary gland invasion.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the complementation experiments with truncated TRP1 mutants.

claim: The N-terminus of TRP1 is the least conserved part of the protein across Plasmodium species.
source: Intriguingly, the N-terminus of TRP1 is the least conserved part of the protein across Plasmodium species (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Strong GFP fluorescence could only be detected in the trp1-gfp line and weak GFP fluorescence in gfp-trp1∆N parasites, while all other lines were non-fluorescent.
source: Interestingly, we could only detect strong GFP fluorescence in the trp1-gfp line and weak GFP fluorescence in gfp-trp1∆N parasites, while all other lines were non-fluorescent (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a primary observation from fluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 5B.

claim: GFP expression in gfp-trp1∆N parasites was only observed in oocysts with already matured sporozoites.
source: In contrast to trp1(-)mCh parasites, which express mCherry early during oocyst formation (Figure 1A), GFP expression in gfp-trp1∆N parasites was only observed in oocysts with already matured sporozoites.
evidence: This is a primary observation from fluorescence microscopy.

claim: TRP1 expression might be post-transcriptionally regulated by the native 3'UTR.
source: This indicates that, beside the transcriptional regulation, TRP1 expression might also be post-transcriptionally regulated by the native 3'UTR, which is not present in trp1(-)mCh parasites.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the differential expression patterns observed.

claim: A gfp:trp1 transcript could be amplified in gfp-trp1comp, gfp-trp1∆N and gfp-trp1∆C sporozoites while no transcript could be detected in wt.
source: We were able to amplify a gfp:trp1 transcript in gfp-trp1comp, gfp-trp1∆N and gfp-trp1∆C sporozoites while no transcript could be detected in wt.
evidence: This is a primary finding from RT-PCR experiments shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Western blotting revealed only a short GFP-fusion protein as well as GFP for the C-terminally tagged full-length TRP1.
source: Finally, we performed Western blotting, which revealed only a short GFP-fusion protein as well as GFP for the C-terminally tagged full-length TRP1 (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from Western blot experiments shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Full-length GFP-TRP1 could not be detected by Western blotting, suggesting that the protein is cleaved.
source: We could not detect full-length GFP-TRP1, suggesting that the protein is cleaved, and also failed to detect protein for the weakly GFP-expressing N-terminal deletion parasites.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Western blot results shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The C-terminal GFP-fusion protein of the full-length TRP1 localized strongly at the periphery of the oocyst.
source: Curiously, the C-terminal GFP-fusion protein of the full-length TRP1 localized strongly at the periphery of the oocyst (Figure 6A, Video 1).
evidence: This is a primary observation from fluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 6A and Video 1.

claim: The GFP-fusion protein of the N-terminally deleted TRP1 did not show localization at the periphery of the oocyst and appeared to accumulate only within the sporozoites.
source: By contrast, the GFP-fusion protein of the N-terminally deleted TRP1 did not show this localization and appeared to accumulate only within the sporozoites (Figure 6B, Video 1).
evidence: This is a primary observation from fluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 6B and Video 1.

claim: The C-terminally tagged TRP1 localized at the periphery towards the rear end of the sporozoite, as well as within the sporozoite at the apical end.
source: Investigation of single sporozoites showed that the C-terminally tagged TRP1 localized at the periphery towards the rear end of the sporozoite, as well as within the sporozoite at the apical end (Figure 7A, Video 2).
evidence: This is a primary observation from fluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 7A and Video 2.

claim: The GFP signal in the gfp-trp1∆N sporozoites localized to membranes within the parasite, presumably the endoplasmatic reticulum (ER).
source: By contrast, the GFP signal in the gfp-trp1∆N sporozoites localized to membranes within the parasite, presumably the endoplasmatic reticulum (ER) as indicated by accumulations around the nucleus (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary observation from fluorescence microscopy with speculative interpretation shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: GFP-TRP1∆N could not be detected on the sporozoite surface using anti-GFP antibodies in fixed sporozoites.
source: By using anti-GFP antibodies in fixed sporozoites, we were not able to detect GFP-TRP1∆N on the sporozoite surface (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from immunofluorescence experiments shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: TRP1-GFP and GFP-TRAP were localized differently.
source: Comparison of the localizations of TRP1-GFP and GFP-TRAP (Kehrer et al., 2016b) showed that the two proteins were localized differently (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a primary observation from comparative fluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 8.

claim: GFP-TRAP appears mostly localized to micronemes at the front end of the sporozoite.
source: While GFP-TRAP appears mostly localized to micronemes at the front end of the sporozoite, TRP1-GFP appears to localize in what might be a subset of micronemes or a different organelle that does not extend all the way to the front.
evidence: This is a primary observation from comparative fluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 8.

claim: TRP1-GFP appears to localize in what might be a subset of micronemes or a different organelle that does not extend all the way to the front.
source: While GFP-TRAP appears mostly localized to micronemes at the front end of the sporozoite, TRP1-GFP appears to localize in what might be a subset of micronemes or a different organelle that does not extend all the way to the front.
evidence: This is a primary observation with speculative interpretation from comparative fluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 8.

claim: TRP1 is transported through the ER.
source: These data together indicate that TRP1 is transported through the ER, is post-translationally processed and can accumulate at the periphery of the parasite on its rear end.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the localization and Western blot data.

claim: TRP1 is post-translationally processed.
source: These data together indicate that TRP1 is transported through the ER, is post-translationally processed and can accumulate at the periphery of the parasite on its rear end.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Western blot data showing only short fusion proteins.

claim: TRP1 can accumulate at the periphery of the parasite on its rear end.
source: These data together indicate that TRP1 is transported through the ER, is post-translationally processed and can accumulate at the periphery of the parasite on its rear end.
evidence: This is a primary observation from fluorescence microscopy.

claim: Sporozoite egress from oocysts was imaged in situ for the first time.
source: Here, we described for the first time the imaging of Plasmodium sporozoite egress from oocysts in situ, which revealed a number of different types of egress events.
evidence: This is a primary methodological achievement of the study.

claim: The imaging revealed a number of different types of egress events.
source: Here, we described for the first time the imaging of Plasmodium sporozoite egress from oocysts in situ, which revealed a number of different types of egress events.
evidence: This is a primary observation from the imaging experiments.

claim: The most striking egress event was the apparent bursting of sporozoites and the apparent budding of sporozoites within vesicle-like deformations of the cyst wall termed sporosomes.
source: The most striking was the apparent bursting of sporozoites and the apparent budding of sporozoites within vesicle-like deformations of the cyst wall that we termed sporosomes (Figure 9C,D; Videos 3 and 7).
evidence: This is a primary observation from the imaging experiments shown in Figure 9C,D and Videos 3 and 7.

claim: Egress events were observed in about 3% of control oocysts.
source: We imaged 547 control oocysts over a total of 16 hr and observed egress events in about 3% of these oocysts, suggesting a rate of 0.5–1 egress events per hour.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the imaging experiments.

claim: The rate of egress events is 0.5–1 egress events per hour.
source: We imaged 547 control oocysts over a total of 16 hr and observed egress events in about 3% of these oocysts, suggesting a rate of 0.5–1 egress events per hour.
evidence: This is calculated from the imaging data.

claim: At the observed rate, 50% of oocysts in a medium infected midgut (~100 oocysts) would be emptied in 2–3 days.
source: At this rate, 50% of oocysts in a medium infected midgut (~100 oocysts) would be emptied in 2–3 days.
evidence: This is calculated from the observed egress rate.

claim: The observed events might well reflect those occurring in vivo.
source: These numbers suggest that the observed events might well reflect those occurring in vivo.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the egress rate calculations.

claim: Sporosome formation was only observed at midguts infected with wild-type parasites.
source: As we only observed sporosome formation at midguts infected with wild-type parasites, it might well be that the oocyst wall is thinned by a succession of parasite-initiated proteolytic events, which are not initiated in trp1(-) or sera5(-) parasites.
evidence: This is a primary observation from the imaging experiments.

claim: The oocyst wall might be thinned by a succession of parasite-initiated proteolytic events, which are not initiated in trp1(-) or sera5(-) parasites.
source: As we only observed sporosome formation at midguts infected with wild-type parasites, it might well be that the oocyst wall is thinned by a succession of parasite-initiated proteolytic events, which are not initiated in trp1(-) or sera5(-) parasites.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the differential egress patterns observed.

claim: EM imaging of sporulated trp1(-)mCh and wild-type oocysts showed no differences in the appearance of the oocyst wall.
source: Yet, EM imaging of sporulated trp1(-)mCh and wild-type oocysts showed no differences in the appearance of the oocyst wall.
evidence: This is a primary observation from electron microscopy experiments shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1.

claim: Even 24 days post infection, trp1(-)mCh oocysts showed little difference in morphology and no difference in oocyst wall thickness when compared to wild-type oocysts 12 days post infection.
source: Even 24 days post infection, trp1(-)mCh oocysts showed little difference in morphology and no difference in oocyst wall thickness when compared to wild-type oocysts 12 days post infection (Figure 10—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary observation from electron microscopy experiments shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1.

claim: Proteolytic degradation of the oocyst wall might not be affected in oocysts lacking TRP1.
source: These observations could suggest that proteolytic degradation of the oocyst wall is not affected in oocysts lacking TRP1.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the electron microscopy observations.

claim: Proteolytic degradation might happen only shortly before or during egress and is therefore hard to observe by electron microscopy in wild-type oocysts.
source: Alternatively, proteolytic degradation might happen only shortly before or during egress and is therefore hard to observe by electron microscopy in wild-type oocysts.
evidence: This is a speculative alternative interpretation of the electron microscopy observations.

claim: TRP1 could lead to sustained microneme secretion that would maintain or initiate gliding motility.
source: Once on the surface, TRP1 could lead, for example, to sustained microneme secretion that would maintain or initiate gliding motility.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about TRP1 function.

claim: TRP1 might play a role in motility by contributing to the disconnection of TRAP from actin filaments at the rear end.
source: Alternatively, it might play a role in motility by contributing to the disconnection of TRAP from actin filaments at the rear end, where the actin filament binding protein coronin was recently also shown to be localized (Bane et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about TRP1 function with citation to a previous study on coronin localization.

claim: In the absence of TRP1, there is no motility within oocysts and possibly reduced secretion.
source: Although these functions remain highly speculative, in the absence of TRP1, there is no motility within oocysts and possibly reduced secretion.
evidence: This is a primary observation from the imaging experiments with speculative interpretation about secretion.

claim: TRP1 could assist in the correct trafficking and secretion of other proteins, as shown for MIC2 and the MIC2-associated protein.
source: Beside the direct interaction with ligands that make contact with the sporozoite surface, TRP1 could also assist in the correct trafficking and secretion of other proteins, as shown for MIC2 and the MIC2-associated protein (Huynh et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about TRP1 function with citation to a previous study on MIC2.

claim: SERA5 is a factor known to be involved in sporozoite egress from oocysts.
source: Clearly, the processes and factors that lead to parasite egress from host cells in general and egress of sporozoites from oocysts in particular are still poorly understood. The factors that are known to date are the serine repeat antigen 5, SERA5 (previously named egress cysteine protease 1; ECP1), the GPI-anchored circumsporozoite protein, CSP (Wang et al., 2005; Aly and Matuschewski, 2005; Tewari et al., 2002), the Plasmodium cysteine repeat modular proteins PCRMP3 and PCRMP4 (Douradinha et al., 2011) and the LCCL-domain-containing proteins PfCCp2 and PfCCp3 (Pradel et al., 2004) (Table 1).
evidence: This is established knowledge with citations to previous studies.

claim: CSP is a factor known to be involved in sporozoite egress from oocysts.
source: Clearly, the processes and factors that lead to parasite egress from host cells in general and egress of sporozoites from oocysts in particular are still poorly understood. The factors that are known to date are the serine repeat antigen 5, SERA5 (previously named egress cysteine protease 1; ECP1), the GPI-anchored circumsporozoite protein, CSP (Wang et al., 2005; Aly and Matuschewski, 2005; Tewari et al., 2002), the Plasmodium cysteine repeat modular proteins PCRMP3 and PCRMP4 (Douradinha et al., 2011) and the LCCL-domain-containing proteins PfCCp2 and PfCCp3 (Pradel et al., 2004) (Table 1).
evidence: This is established knowledge with citations to previous studies.

claim: PCRMP3 and PCRMP4 are factors known to be involved in sporozoite egress from oocysts.
source: Clearly, the processes and factors that lead to parasite egress from host cells in general and egress of sporozoites from oocysts in particular are still poorly understood. The factors that are known to date are the serine repeat antigen 5, SERA5 (previously named egress cysteine protease 1; ECP1), the GPI-anchored circumsporozoite protein, CSP (Wang et al., 2005; Aly and Matuschewski, 2005; Tewari et al., 2002), the Plasmodium cysteine repeat modular proteins PCRMP3 and PCRMP4 (Douradinha et al., 2011) and the LCCL-domain-containing proteins PfCCp2 and PfCCp3 (Pradel et al., 2004) (Table 1).
evidence: This is established knowledge with citations to previous studies.

claim: PfCCp2 and PfCCp3 are factors known to be involved in sporozoite egress from oocysts.
source: Clearly, the processes and factors that lead to parasite egress from host cells in general and egress of sporozoites from oocysts in particular are still poorly understood. The factors that are known to date are the serine repeat antigen 5, SERA5 (previously named egress cysteine protease 1; ECP1), the GPI-anchored circumsporozoite protein, CSP (Wang et al., 2005; Aly and Matuschewski, 2005; Tewari et al., 2002), the Plasmodium cysteine repeat modular proteins PCRMP3 and PCRMP4 (Douradinha et al., 2011) and the LCCL-domain-containing proteins PfCCp2 and PfCCp3 (Pradel et al., 2004) (Table 1).
evidence: This is established knowledge with citations to previous studies.

claim: Sporozoites lacking SERA5, PCRMP3, PCRMP4, PfCCp2 and PfCCp3 fail to egress from oocysts.
source: Sporozoites lacking SERA5, PCRMP3, PCRMP4, PfCCp2 and PfCCp3 fail to egress from oocysts (Aly and Matuschewski, 2005; Douradinha et al., 2011; Pradel et al., 2004), whereas parasites lacking CSP do not complete sporozoite formation (Ménard et al., 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge with citations to previous studies.

claim: Parasites lacking CSP do not complete sporozoite formation.
source: Sporozoites lacking SERA5, PCRMP3, PCRMP4, PfCCp2 and PfCCp3 fail to egress from oocysts (Aly and Matuschewski, 2005; Douradinha et al., 2011; Pradel et al., 2004), whereas parasites lacking CSP do not complete sporozoite formation (Ménard et al., 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge with citation to a previous study.

claim: The change of four basic amino acids into alanines within region II+ of CSP allowed normal sporozoite development but blocked egress from oocysts.
source: The change of four basic amino acids into alanines within region II+ of CSP allowed normal sporozoite development but blocked egress from oocysts (Wang et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge with citation to a previous study.

claim: All six mutant parasites lines (lacking SERA5, PCRMP3, PCRMP4, PfCCp2, PfCCp3, or with CSP mutations) retained their capacity to migrate actively once sporozoites were mechanically released from oocysts.
source: All six mutant parasites lines retained their capacity to migrate actively once sporozoites were mechanically released from oocysts (Table 1).
evidence: This is established knowledge summarized in Table 1.

claim: Parasites that lack SIAP-1 have a strongly reduced rate of sporozoites egressing from oocysts but are still able to enter into salivary glands in low numbers.
source: Another protein, the sporozoite invasion associated protein-1 (SIAP-1), possesses no recognizable structural or functional domains but has been identified as having a partial role in sporozoite egress. Parasites that lack SIAP-1 have a strongly reduced rate of sporozoites egressing from oocysts but are still able to enter into salivary glands in low numbers (Engelmann et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge with citation to a previous study.

claim: SIAP-1 knockout sporozoites fail to undergo efficient gliding motility.
source: In contrast to parasite lines that lack the previously mentioned proteins (SERA5, PCRMP 3 and 4, PfCCp 2 and 3) or parasite lines that contain specific mutations within CSP, SIAP-1 knockout sporozoites also fail to undergo efficient gliding motility (Engelmann et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge with citation to a previous study.

claim: GAMA has been shown to be essential for egress from oocysts.
source: Similarly, the GPI-anchored micronemal antigen GAMA (previously named PSOP9) has been shown to be essential for egress from oocysts.
evidence: This is established knowledge with implicit citation to previous studies.

claim: Sporozoites that lack GAMA are not able to perform gliding motility in vitro and within oocysts ex vivo.
source: Sporozoites that lack GAMA are also not able to perform gliding motility in vitro and within oocysts ex vivo (Ecker et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge with citation to a previous study.

claim: GAMA is expressed in all Plasmodium stages that contain micronemes.
source: Interestingly, GAMA is expressed in all Plasmodium stages that contain micronemes and has been discussed as a potential vaccine candidate against blood stages (Hinds et al., 2009; Arumugam et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge with citations to previous studies.

claim: It is unlikely that GAMA has a specific function in sporozoite egress from oocysts.
source: This ubiquitous expression profile makes it unlikely that GAMA has a specific function in sporozoite egress from oocysts but suggests that it is important for egress and invasion in general.
evidence: This is an inference based on the ubiquitous expression pattern of GAMA.

claim: GAMA is important for egress and invasion in general.
source: This ubiquitous expression profile makes it unlikely that GAMA has a specific function in sporozoite egress from oocysts but suggests that it is important for egress and invasion in general.
evidence: This is an inference based on the ubiquitous expression pattern of GAMA.

claim: The egress defect of gama(-) sporozoites presumably causes a defect within the micronemes.
source: Therefore the egress defect of gama(-) sporozoites presumably causes a defect within the micronemes that has more or less impact dependent on the observed parasite stage.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the GAMA knockout phenotype.

claim: gama(-) ookinetes produce 78% fewer oocysts than wild-type ookinetes.
source: This hypothesis is supported by the observation that gama(-) ookinetes produce 78% fewer oocysts than wild-type ookinetes, indicating that the loss of GAMA has an effect prior to oocyst development.
evidence: This is established knowledge with implicit citation to previous studies.

claim: Two different pathways, involving either intracellular or extracellular signals, might trigger the release of sporozoites from their oocyst.
source: We speculate that two different pathways, involving either intracellular or extracellular signals, might trigger the release of sporozoites from their oocyst.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: The intracellular pathway might require quorum sensing between the sporozoites of an oocyst.
source: The intracellular pathway might require quorum sensing between the sporozoites of an oocyst that reponds to the presence or absence of a specific factor once sporulation is completed.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: The extracellular pathway might be initiated by the permeabilization of the oocyst wall.
source: The extracellular pathway might be initiated by the permeabilization of the oocyst wall, either by intracellular factors that are secreted after sporulation or by the breakdown of the oocyst wall that is not longer maintained once sporulation is completed.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: Degradation of the oocyst wall is probably an interplay of multiple factors.
source: Independent of the pathway that triggers sporozoite egress, degradation of the oocyst wall is probably an interplay of multiple factors that do not lead to a uniform breakdown of the oocyst envelope but create focal weakenings that enable local release of sporozoites or budding of sporosomes (Figure 10).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the egress observations shown in Figure 10.

claim: sera5(-) parasites showed about four and eight times more oocysts with motile sporozoites than wild-type oocysts in both assays.
source: Intriguingly, sera5(-) parasites showed about four and eight times more oocysts with motile sporozoites than wild-type oocysts in both assays (Figure 9A,B), respectively.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the imaging experiments shown in Figure 9A,B.

claim: Motility precedes egress.
source: Considering that sera5(-) sporozoites do not exit oocysts, this further suggests that motility precedes egress.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that sera5(-) parasites show increased motility but no egress.
